questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Count oxygen atoms in a glycosidic bond
questions.stem: Working the problem, a glycosidic bond joins two sugars through an oxygen bridge. How many oxygen atoms form the bridge itself?
questions.explanation: A glycosidic bond is an acetal linkage in which a single oxygen atom bridges the anomeric carbon of one sugar and a carbon of the other sugar or an aglycone.
questions.hint: One bridging oxygen per glycosidic bond.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Count glucose units in a disaccharide
questions.stem: Working the problem, how many monosaccharide units does a disaccharide contain?
questions.explanation: A disaccharide contains two monosaccharide units joined by a glycosidic bond, such as sucrose which joins glucose and fructose.
questions.hint: Disaccharide means two sugar units.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Working the problem, a Kiliani-Fischer synthesis applied to an aldopentose gives aldohexoses with how many carbons?
questions.explanation: Kiliani-Fischer adds one carbon to the chain, so an aldopentose with five carbons gives a pair of aldohexoses with six carbons each.
questions.hint: Five plus one equals six.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Working the problem, for a given sugar forming a pyranose ring, how many anomers differ only at the anomeric carbon?
questions.explanation: Formation of the hemiacetal creates a new stereocenter at the anomeric carbon, giving two anomers called alpha and beta that differ only in the configuration at that carbon.
questions.hint: Alpha and beta are the two anomers.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: For the formula, how many stereocenters does open-chain D-glucose contain?
questions.explanation: Open-chain glucose has stereocenters at carbons two, three, four and five, giving four, while carbon one is the aldehyde carbonyl and carbon six is a primary alcohol.
questions.hint: Count the chiral carbons in the open chain.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Count atoms in a glucopyranose ring
questions.stem: For the formula, how many atoms form the ring of glucopyranose?
questions.explanation: Glucopyranose forms a six-membered ring containing five carbons and one oxygen, resulting from attack of the carbon five hydroxyl on the aldehyde at carbon one.
questions.hint: Five carbons plus one oxygen gives six.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Explain the following: why does pure alpha-D-glucose show mutarotation in water?

answer.exemplar: In water the hemiacetal ring of alpha-D-glucose opens to the achiral-at-anomeric-carbon aldehyde form, which can reclose with either face of the carbonyl attacked by the carbon five hydroxyl, producing a mixture of alpha and beta anomers; the changing proportions change the observed optical rotation until equilibrium is reached.

questions.explanation: Ring opening allows both anomers to form. In water the hemiacetal ring of alpha-D-glucose opens to the achiral-at-anomeric-carbon aldehyde form, which can reclose with either face of the carbonyl attacked by the carbon five hydroxyl, producing a mixture of alpha and beta anomers; the changing proportions change the observed optical rotation until equilibrium is reached.
questions.hint: Equilibrium rotation reflects the anomer mixture.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Explain the following: why is maltose reducing while sucrose is not?

answer.exemplar: Maltose has one free anomeric hemiacetal that can open to an aldehyde, so it reduces Tollens and Benedict reagents; sucrose links the anomeric carbon of glucose to the anomeric carbon of fructose in a glycosidic bond, so neither anomeric center can open and sucrose is nonreducing.

questions.explanation: One free anomeric carbon makes maltose reducing. Maltose has one free anomeric hemiacetal that can open to an aldehyde, so it reduces Tollens and Benedict reagents; sucrose links the anomeric carbon of glucose to the anomeric carbon of fructose in a glycosidic bond, so neither anomeric center can open and sucrose is nonreducing.
questions.hint: Both anomeric carbons are tied up in sucrose.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Explain the following: why can humans digest starch but not cellulose?

answer.exemplar: Human enzymes recognize alpha glycosidic linkages and hydrolyze them, but cellulose has beta-1,4 linkages whose geometry is not complementary to those enzymes; the same glucose units are connected with different stereochemistry, producing a very different polymer shape that our enzymes cannot cleave.

questions.explanation: Enzymes are stereospecific for alpha linkages. Human enzymes recognize alpha glycosidic linkages and hydrolyze them, but cellulose has beta-1,4 linkages whose geometry is not complementary to those enzymes; the same glucose units are connected with different stereochemistry, producing a very different polymer shape that our enzymes cannot cleave.
questions.hint: Beta links give a different polymer geometry.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Explain the following: why do glucose, mannose and fructose give the same osazone?

answer.exemplar: Osazone formation modifies the carbonyl carbon and the adjacent carbon two, erasing the stereochemical differences between glucose and mannose at carbon two, while fructose's carbonyl at carbon two is converted to the same structure after tautomerization, so all three converge on the same crystalline osazone.

questions.explanation: Carbons one and two are converted identically. Osazone formation modifies the carbonyl carbon and the adjacent carbon two, erasing the stereochemical differences between glucose and mannose at carbon two, while fructose's carbonyl at carbon two is converted to the same structure after tautomerization, so all three converge on the same crystalline osazone.
questions.hint: Differences at those carbons are erased.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: In a research note, what is the dominant form of a neutral amino acid in water at neutral pH?

options.text: A neutral molecule with NH2 and COOH
options.misconception: internal proton transfer forms the zwitterion

options.text: An anion with a deprotonated amine
options.misconception: the amine is protonated near neutral pH

options.text: A cation with a protonated carboxyl
options.misconception: the carboxyl is deprotonated near neutral pH

options.text: A zwitterion with a protonated ammonium and a deprotonated carboxylate

questions.explanation: At neutral pH an amino acid exists mainly as a zwitterion bearing a positively charged ammonium group and a negatively charged carboxylate group, giving it a net charge near zero and high water solubility.

zero is the net charge at the pI

options.misconception: internal proton transfer forms the zwitterion

options.text: A zwitterion with a protonated ammonium and a deprotonated carboxylate
An anion with a deprotonated amine
options.misconception: the amine is protonated near neutral pH

options.text: A cation with a protonated carboxyl
options.misconception: the carboxyl is deprotonated near neutral pH

questions.explanation: At neutral pH an amino acid exists mainly as a zwitterion bearing a positively charged ammonium group and a negatively charged carboxylate group, giving it a net charge near zero and high water solubility.
questions.hint: Internal proton transfer gives plus and minus charges.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: In a tutorial session, what is the net charge of an amino acid at a pH above its isoelectric point?

options.misconception: below the pI it is positive
zero is the net charge at the pI

questions.explanation: At pH above the isoelectric point the solution is more basic than the pI, so the ammonium group loses a proton and the molecule carries a net negative charge and migrates toward the anode in electrophoresis.
questions.hint: Above pI means net negative charge.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: You are given the following: which amino acid has a positively charged side chain at neutral pH?
questions.explanation: Lysine has a side chain amino group with a pKa around 10.5 that is protonated and positively charged at neutral pH, while aspartic acid is deprotonated and negative and serine or valine are uncharged.
questions.hint: Lysine side chain is basic.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: In a synthesis planning session, what is the structural unit linking amino acids in a peptide?

options.text: An amide bond between the carboxyl of one and the amino of another
A disulfide bond only between all residues
options.misconception: disulfides are cross-links, not the backbone

questions.explanation: A peptide bond is an amide linkage formed by condensation of the carboxyl group of one amino acid with the amino group of another, and its partial double-bond character makes the peptide unit planar.
questions.hint: Peptide bond is an amide.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: A laboratory report asks: which method removes one residue at a time from the N-terminus of a peptide?
questions.explanation: Edman degradation reacts the N-terminal amino group with phenylisothiocyanate and cleaves the labeled residue as a phenylthiohydantoin derivative under acid conditions, allowing sequential identification from the N-terminus.
questions.hint: Edman steps from the N-terminus.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: For this reaction scenario, which interaction stabilizes an alpha helix in proteins?

options.text: Ionic bonds between side chains only
Hydrogen bonds between backbone carbonyl and N-H groups

options.misconception: the backbone is linked by peptide bonds, but helices are stabilized by H-bonds

questions.explanation: An alpha helix is stabilized by hydrogen bonds between the carbonyl oxygen of one residue and the N-H of a residue four positions later, forming a regular repeating pattern along the backbone.
questions.hint: Backbone hydrogen bonds stabilize helices.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: In the laboratory (example), why is direct condensation of two amino acids difficult without protecting groups?

options.text: Peptide bonds form too slowly at any pH
Amino and carboxyl groups can react in unwanted combinations

questions.explanation: Without protection the amino group of one amino acid can react with its own carboxyl or with the wrong partner, and carboxyl groups must be activated, so protecting groups and coupling agents are used to control which bonds form.
questions.hint: Chemoselectivity requires protection and activation.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Which of the following is an essential amino acid for humans?
questions.explanation: Leucine is one of the essential amino acids that humans cannot synthesize de novo and must obtain from the diet, along with isoleucine, valine, lysine and others.
questions.hint: Leucine must come from the diet.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Predict pI of an acidic amino acid
questions.stem: While planning the experiment, for an amino acid with an acidic side chain, is its isoelectric point above or below neutral pH?

options.misconception: basic side chains raise the pI
all amino acids have a pI

questions.explanation: An acidic side chain adds an extra carboxyl group, so an additional deprotonation is needed to reach the neutral species, which occurs at an acidic pH, giving a pI below seven.
questions.hint: Acidic side chain lowers the pI.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: In a research note, which stereochemical family do the commonly occurring protein amino acids belong to, excluding glycine?

options.misconception: protein amino acids are mostly L

questions.explanation: All the common proteinogenic amino acids except glycine have the L configuration at the alpha carbon, reflecting the homochirality of biologicalProtein, while D-amino acids occur in some bacterial cell walls.
questions.hint: Protein amino acids are L.
